data.title: Joint Electricity Price and Load Forecasting for Data Center Battery Dispatch Using Polynomial Diffusion Models
data.description: The rapid growth of large-scale data centers (DCs) is increasing electricity demand, market volatility, and operating costs. Battery energy storage systems (BESSs) can mitigate these challenges by shifting electricity purchases from high-price to low-price periods. This paper proposes a real-time BESS dispatch framework using polynomial diffusion models (PDMs) to forecast both electricity prices and DC loads. Leveraging the closed-form conditional expectations of PDMs, the forecasts are integrated into a dynamic programming (DP) framework to minimize electricity procurement costs. Across the evaluated BESS configurations, the proposed approach achieves 2.63 times the cost savings of a rule-based (RB) strategy.
data.author: Matthew Van Ham, Yiping Liu, Xiaozhe Wang

data.title: A Critical Review of Grid Integration Challenges and Flexibility Opportunities for Large-Scale Data Centers
data.description: The rapid proliferation of cloud computing and artificial intelligence workloads is fundamentally reshaping the magnitude, spatial concentration, and electrical characteristics of data center power demand. Data centers differ from conventional commercial loads because they combine high rack densities, converter-dominated interfaces, thermally coupled cooling, uninterruptible power supplies, programmable workloads, and increasingly complex behind-the-meter generation and storage within a single facility. This review examines their grid integration from utility and sustainable-energy perspectives across resource planning, large-load interconnection, distribution feeders, market operation, real-time dynamics, power quality, and asset management. Particular attention is given to distribution-level issues that receive limited treatment in broader energy reviews: bidirectional operation on renewable-rich feeders, harmonic propagation and resonance, ride-through and reconnection, transformer derating, cable ampacity, neutral-conductor heating, protection, and measurement. Static, composite, physics-based dynamic, calibrated, impedance, electromagnetic transient, and hybrid load models are compared according to study purpose and data requirements, and utility coordination platforms, uninterruptible power supply and battery control, workload flexibility, renewable co-location, cogeneration, fuel cells, thermal storage, and clean firm supply are assessed. The central finding is that requested peak demand and annual energy matching alone cannot establish reliable or sustainable integration. Credible assessment must consider hourly and locational supply, network deliverability, marginal emissions, lifecycle and water impacts, backup obligations, rebound, asset health, and verified operating capability.
data.author: Bibek Dhakal, Manohar Chamana, Biswambhar Gayen, Jatendar Kumar, S M Shams Rahman, Aaqib Peerzada, Ki Yeob Lee, Olatunji M. Adeyanju, Bhaskar Mitra, Stephen Bayne

data.title: Dynamic Modeling of Transmission Networks, Grid-Following Inverters, and UPS-Based AI Data Centers
data.description: This document presents dynamic models of a transmission network and average models of power-electronic devices and loads in the synchronous $dq$ frame. We model the network in the positive sequence and its synchronous generators with the classical swing equation and a first-order turbine governor. The power-electronic models cover grid-following inverters and AI data centers. Each inverter has a phase-locked loop, a power controller, and a current controller. Each data center connects to the grid through two step-down transformers. Its low-voltage bus feeds an IT load, an induction-motor cooling load, and a constant-impedance load. A double-conversion uninterruptible power supply (UPS) serves the IT load. We model its rectifier, grid-forming output inverter, battery, and bidirectional DC-DC converter. A measured GPU power trace drives the IT demand. We replace every non-smooth operation with a smooth surrogate. This keeps the discretized model continuously differentiable for the nonlinear solver. We also show how we initialize each model at its power-flow operating point.
data.author: Muhammad Hamza Ali, Amritanshu Pandey

data.title: Estimating data center water use: Best practices and critical questions
data.description: Concerns are growing about the water use of data centers. To quantify the scales, drivers, and possible trajectories of this water use, analytical estimation is required. However, current estimation methods and results vary widely due, in part, to a lack of established best practices. This variance is illustrated with a U.S. case study demonstrating a roughly 24-fold difference in possible outcomes based on observed U.S. study design variations. To address these challenges, this review synthesizes 14 best practices for advancing the science and utility of data center water use estimation. These proposed best practices can also be used as critical questions for stakeholders when evaluating the quality of any study. Using a structured rubric, it further assesses the literature to date (31 studies) against these best practices. The assessment reveals important opportunities for improvement and standardization in future study scopes, clarity, methods, and scientific knowledge building utility. It further finds that, while many studies provide reasonable transparency, scope definitions, replicability, and uncertainty treatment, many fall short in scientific justification, data representativeness, transparency on hydropower assumptions, terminological consistency, and meaningful discussions of limitations and future work. Recommendations are proposed for analysts, stakeholders, and policymakers to leverage these findings to help build a vibrant data center water use research community. Finally, this review can also be used as a basic primer for understanding data center cooling configurations and water use among analysts, policymakers, the media, and the public.
data.author: Eric Masanet

data.title: Halley: A Predictive Control Plane for Optical AI Data Center Networks
data.description: A frontier AI model is trained in an AI data center, on tens of thousands of accelerators joined by a dedicated network, and every training step ends with all of them exchanging data at once. Between racks, that network is optical, and each of its four layers, from lasers to switches, runs a fixed or after-the-fact policy. Lasers sharing an enclosure, cooling, and power can fail together. At a fixed spare ratio, correlated failure provably caps a pool's availability however large it grows. In this paper, we present a comprehensive predictive control plane framework, called Halley, that reads each resource's next state and acts before the failure occurs. It has four components, each carrying a formal guarantee: LightReserve that sizes the laser pool to provide a coverage bound, FoldFit that schedules the switch within $11/9$ of the optimal, ThermaLead that holds a microring with one-step-ahead control, and TriageGuard that protects the highest-risk modules first. Halley gives each layer a predictive controller that defers to the deployed policy when unsure. Composed from simulations at that point, effective goodput, the share of ideal throughput kept, rises from 65.2\% to 76.5\% if a window that exhausts its spares is lost. If only the dark channels' bandwidth is lost, it reaches 67.4\%. Per megawatt, that is up to 1.03--1.17 times the training; for the same training, up to 3.3--14.7\% less data center capacity. \textsf{Halley}'s fallback circuits are formally verified and are shown to achieve close timing on a commercial FPGA, and pass a 130~nm signoff.
data.author: Manav Mishra, Krishna M. Sivalingam

data.title: Identifiability-Guided Composite Load Modeling of AI Data Centers
data.description: The rapid growth of AI data centers introduces large, workload-dependent loads whose protection and reconnection behavior can affect power-system transient stability. Calibrating dynamic models of such loads is challenging because treating all associated elements as freely estimable may lead to weakly identified or physically confounded parameterizations. This paper proposes an identifiability-guided calibration framework for a composite load model with separate IT, cooling, and auxiliary branches. A nuisance-projected Fisher-information criterion characterizes the local identifiability of the cooling-motor composition, while a workload non-equivalence result shows that voltage-only recalibration cannot reproduce workload-dependent responses. Guided by these results, a grey-box estimator trained with branch-level supervision learns the workload-to-power relation and the cooling composition, while retaining a prescribed UPS protection law and an externally anchored reconnect-ramp duration. The learned workload relation is then distilled into a closed form for transient-stability simulation. Evaluation using 300,000 MIT Supercloud GPU power-utilization samples and 12,600 IEEE 39-bus fault scenarios yields an aggregate active-power $R^2$ of 0.948, compared with 0.856 for an LSTM baseline. Removing branch-level supervision preserves relatively high aggregate accuracy but substantially degrades cooling-component recovery. Under unseen deep voltage sags, the proposed model achieves a transient $R^2$ of 0.750, compared with 0.033 for the LSTM. Closed-loop simulations further show that cooling composition and protection behavior can affect retained-load states and voltage responses near protection thresholds.
data.author: Ding Lin, Jianhui Wang, Meng Yue, Tianqiao Zhao

data.answer:
Recent developments point to tighter integration of liquid cooling with whole-facility simulation and control. One study adds a native EnergyPlus object for direct-to-chip liquid cooling that models chilled-water and warm-water architectures, secondary loops, coolant distribution units, and chip temperatures in one solver; it reports validation against Modelica and finds warm-water liquid cooling can reduce annual PUE from 1.43 to 1.25 while eliminating on-site water use and cutting total facility energy by 37.9% in the case study. [1]

Operationally, liquid cooling is making measurement and monitoring more important, with emphasis on precise real-time sensing across both liquid and air environments, and retrofits are being viewed as beneficial but case-specific because cost, downtime, and infrastructure constraints limit where they make sense. [2] [3]

On the power-management side, the latest coverage emphasizes smarter integrated control: AI-driven data centers are described as needing coordinated sensing, motor control, and power management in a single responsive, failure-anticipating system. A broader grid-integration review also highlights how large data centers are reshaping electrical demand and creating challenges around interconnection, distribution feeders, power quality, and asset management, especially given converter-dominated interfaces and tightly coupled cooling and backup systems. [4] [5]
